title: The Rule of Carmel
hookLine: stay in your cell, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord

lines: HERMITS ASK FOR A WAY OF LIFE.
cards: Good intentions only get a group of hermits so far. The men on Carmel had come to pray, and now there were several of them, sharing a spring and a hillside. They needed to know how to live.
So, the text tells us, they asked for a way of life in writing, from Albert, the patriarch of Jerusalem. What came back wasn't a thick book of regulations.
It reads like a letter, addressed to the hermits living near the spring on Mount Carmel, and in the middle of it sits one sentence that holds the rest together.

teach.h: FIRST THE GOAL: ALLEGIANCE TO CHRIST.
teach.b: The Rule of Carmel opens with the goal before any rules: to live in allegiance to Jesus Christ and serve him with a pure heart.

teach.h: A CELL, AN ORATORY, WORK, SILENCE.
teach.b: Each hermit gets a cell of his own. An oratory stands in the middle of the cells, where they gather for Mass. They work with their hands.

teach.h: STAY IN YOUR CELL, OR NEAR IT.
teach.b: And then the sentence: each one is to stay in his cell, or near it, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord and keeping watch in prayer, unless some other duty calls him away.
Anyone who prays the Psalms hears the echo. Psalm one, in the Douay-Rheims: "on his law he shall meditate day and night." The Rule gives the psalm an address: a small room.
Jesus gives it a door, in Matthew: "enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret." The cell is not a prison; the Rule says nothing about locking anyone in.
The instruction is to stay, which is harder, because staying is a choice made again every hour.

teach.h: UNLESS A DUTY CALLS: GO, THEN RETURN.
teach.b: And notice the word unless. The Rule expects interruptions: work, a brother who needs help, the business of the house.

teach.h: ON HIS LAW HE SHALL MEDITATE DAY AND NIGHT.
teach.b: The hermit goes, does what's needed, and comes back. The cell is home base, not a hiding place. The Rule promises no quick results.
It asks the hermit to come back, again and again, to the same small room, and keep watch there in prayer.

how: Carmelite friars and nuns still take the Rule of Saint Albert as their foundation, and in their houses each has a cell for prayer and rest, with an oratory or chapel at the center of community life.

games.q: you're a hermit on Carmel, praying in your cell, and a brother needs help hauling water. the rule says stay in your cell. what do you do?
o: stay put. the rule is the rule.

games.why: the rule says stay in your cell "unless" another duty calls. the cell is home base: you go, do what's needed, and return.

practice: Let the room you're in be your cell for a little while, and don't get up for anything.
If you pray, pray the psalm's line slowly or sit before God without words; if you don't, rest your attention on the room itself, its sounds, its light, the chair under you.
When the urge comes to check something or fetch something, notice it, and stay.

wordCard.voice: The Rule of Carmel. A letter of life for the hermits on the mountain, with one sentence at its center: stay in your cell, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language of the Rule: a small room. the hermit's cell, and the one place the Rule asks him to stay.
